reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of ACADVL affecting the first dehydrogenation step for long-chain (C14-C20) acyl-CoA substrates at the inner mitochondrial membrane

Presents as a clinical spectrum: a severe early-onset cardiac form with cardiomyopathy and hypoglycaemia, a hepatic/hypoglycaemic infantile form, and a milder later-onset myopathic form with exertional rhabdomyolysis
Newborn screening hallmark is an elevated tetradecenoylcarnitine (C14:1), often with raised C14 and C14:2 species
Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia occurs with fasting or illness, similar to other long-chain oxidation defects
Older children and adults typically present with exercise-induced muscle pain, myoglobinuria and creatine kinase rises rather than hypoglycaemia
Dietary strategy limits long-chain fat and substitutes medium-chain triglyceride as an energy source, alongside fasting avoidance and an emergency illness regimen
Pre-exertion carbohydrate and avoidance of prolonged strenuous activity reduce rhabdomyolysis in the myopathic phenotype
reference.pathophysiology: Very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase is bound to the inner mitochondrial membrane and initiates beta-oxidation of long-chain fatty acyl-CoA esters. Loss of activity blocks energy production from long-chain fat during fasting, exercise or catabolic stress, so the heart and skeletal muscle, which rely heavily on fatty-acid oxidation, are particularly vulnerable, and hepatic ketogenesis fails during fasting. Accumulating long-chain acyl-CoA and acylcarnitine intermediates are thought to be arrhythmogenic and myotoxic, and residual enzyme activity largely determines whether the phenotype is severe and cardiac or mild and myopathic.
additionalDifferentials: Other long-chain oxidation defects (LCHAD/mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency)
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency (myopathic rhabdomyolysis phenotype)
MCAD deficiency and other short/medium-chain oxidation defects
Primary dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of other cause
Metabolic myopathies including glycogenoses presenting with exertional intolerance
Sepsis or myocarditis in an infant with cardiac decompensation
additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile showing elevated C14:1 and related long-chain species
Creatine kinase and urinary myoglobin during suspected rhabdomyolysis
Blood glucose, ketones, ammonia and lactate during acute illness
Echocardiography and ECG when a cardiac phenotype is suspected
ACADVL molecular genetic testing for confirmation
Fibroblast fatty-acid oxidation flux studies or enzyme assay where needed
redFlags: Cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia or pericardial effusion in a decompensating infant
Pigmenturia with markedly raised creatine kinase indicating rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury risk
Rapid clinical deterioration during intercurrent illness or after prolonged exercise
reference.prognosis: The severe neonatal cardiac form historically carried high mortality, but screen-detected diagnosis with early dietary management has improved outcomes; the myopathic form is compatible with normal life expectancy provided rhabdomyolysis triggers are avoided.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis in an adult presenting only with exertional muscle symptoms
Using unrestricted long-chain fat rather than medium-chain triglyceride substitution
Failing to give generous carbohydrate during illness or before prolonged exercise
Missing evolving cardiomyopathy because the initial presentation was hypoglycaemia
references: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
